passages.text: Then, seeing that the crowd had come in, Peter sat down, told us to sit beside him, and began his instruction, first persuading us of the reason why he had sent us ahead from the baptism and had himself arrived late. He gave the following reason: “As soon as you withdrew,” he said, “an old laborer came in with us, inquisitively concealing himself. Having watched us beforehand, as he later admitted, to see what we would do when we entered the sheltered place, he came out secretly and followed. At a suitable place he approached, greeted me, and said, ‘I have followed you for a long time, wanting to speak with you, but I was ashamed, lest you be angry at me for being inquisitive. Now, if you wish, I will tell you what seems true to me.’ I answered, ‘Tell us what you think is good, and we will welcome you, even if what is said is not actually good, since with a good intention you have wanted to say what seems good to you.’”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive use of “steal” means hiding or stealing along rather than theft of property. The note preserves the figurative wording’s furtiveness.
The object is the man, not necessarily an endorsement of the truth of his statement, as the following concession makes clear.

lexical_decisions.chosen: began his instruction, first persuading us
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the guiding explanation of ὑφηγεῖται and the persuasive force of πείθων are represented. The latter can mean satisfying or convincing the listeners concerning the reason; it is not reduced to merely providing information.

passages.text: “As we were saying such things to one another, a large crowd gathered. Then, looking at the crowd, I said, ‘I and my people have inherited from our ancestors the worship of God and have a command not to attend to natal destiny—I mean the discipline of astrology. For this reason I have paid it no attention. Thus I am not experienced in astrology; I will explain the things in which I am experienced. Since I cannot refute natal destiny from the very science concerning natal destiny, I wish to demonstrate in another way that affairs are governed by providence, and that everyone will receive honor or punishment according to what he does. Whether now or later makes no difference to me, provided that everyone will certainly receive the consequences of what he has done. Here is the proof that natal destiny does not exist. If someone standing here lacks eyes, has a crippled hand, a lame foot, or some other bodily condition that has no possibility of returning to health and lies beyond every profession of healing—someone whom even astrologers do not profess to heal, because nothing of this sort has happened throughout the long span of time—and I, by petitioning God, provide the healing, when such a condition could never obtain correction through natal destiny: if this happens in this way, are not those who blaspheme the God who made everything doing wrong?’ The old man answered, ‘Is saying that everything is subject to natal destiny blasphemy?’ I answered, ‘Very much so. For if all people’s sins, acts of impiety, and licentious deeds come from stars, and the stars were appointed by God to do these things, so that they bring about every grievous thing, everyone’s sins are referred back to him who placed natal destiny in the stars.’”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The source denotes a people or tribe; its proper name is not supplied in the English.
This can refer to every promise or claim of healing as well as a healing occupation. The main text keeps the claim that the condition lies beyond professed healing ability.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁπότε ἐκ γενέσεως κατόρθωσιν τὸ τοιοῦτο οὐδέποτε λαβεῖν ἠδυνήθη
lexical_decisions.chosen: when such a condition could never obtain correction through natal destiny
lexical_decisions.rationale: The hypothetical demonstration’s premise is retained as Peter’s argument. No actual present healing or empirical validation is asserted by the translation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν οὐδὲ ἀστρολόγοι ἰᾶσθαι ἐπαγγέλλονται, ὅτι μὴ ἀπὸ τοῦ μακροῦ αἰῶνος τοιοῦτόν τι γέγονεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: someone whom even astrologers do not profess to heal, because nothing of this sort has happened throughout the long span of time
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text reads ὅτι causally and μὴ as negating γέγονεν: the lack of precedent explains the absence of astrologers’ healing claims. The following statement that such correction never occurred through natal destiny supports that linkage. A material alternative takes ὅτι μὴ as an exception marker: “someone whom even astrologers do not profess to heal, except insofar as something of this sort has occurred since long ago.” That reading qualifies their claims by admitting an exception tied to historical precedent, rather than supplying the categorical causal denial in the main text. The supplied μὴ is retained, not silently corrected to οὐ; this is a disclosed attachment choice, not a transcription defect.

passages.text: “The old man answered, ‘You have truly spoken greatly, but my own awareness stands in the way of all your incomparable proof. For I am an astrologer, and formerly lived in Rome. Becoming friends with someone related to Caesar, I knew precisely his natal configuration and that of his wife, and I observed their deeds actually fulfilled in accordance with their natal destiny. I cannot be persuaded by your argument. For the arrangement of her nativity was one that produces adulteresses who fall in love with their own servants and die in water abroad. And this is just what happened: falling in love with her own servant and unable to bear the reproach, she fled with him, lodged in a foreign land, shared his bed, and perished at sea.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: my own awareness stands in the way
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνείδησις can mean conscience or personal knowledge/awareness. His ensuing firsthand account supports awareness, not a modern clinical diagnosis.

The source’s servants have bonded status and belong to the women’s households. “Slaves” would make the legal ownership more explicit; “servants” follows the supplied POB policy while this note preserves ownership and dependency.
The word describes the configuration of the nativity, not a clinical disposition. “Horoscopic configuration” is the more technical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φυγοῦσα σὺν αὐτῷ, ἐν ἀλλοδαπῇ ὁρμήσασα
lexical_decisions.chosen: she fled with him, lodged in a foreign land
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text reads ὁρμήσασα in the lodging or anchoring sense of ὁρμέω: she stopped or stayed in the foreign land. ἐν ἀλλοδαπῇ is the location of that action, not its destination. The form can alternatively be read from ὁρμάω as setting out or moving, giving “having set out in a foreign land.” The narration of flight followed by sharing a bed supports lodging as the main contextual choice, without asserting it uniquely or changing the Greek.

passages.text: “After the old man said this, I understood from his account that the old man he said had died was your father. I did not wish to bring up your circumstances with him until I had consulted you. But after learning where he was staying and telling him where I was staying, for accuracy’s sake I asked only this: ‘What was the old man’s name?’ He said, ‘Faustus.’ ‘And his twin sons’ names?’ He answered, ‘Faustinus and Faustinianus.’ ‘And the third son’s?’ He said, ‘Clement.’ ‘And what was the name of their mother?’ He said, ‘Mattidia.’ So, moved to tears by sympathy, I dismissed the crowds and came to you, so that after sharing the salt I might consult you about these things. I did not want to tell you before we partook of salt, lest, overcome by grief, you spend the day of baptism in mourning, when even angels rejoice.” While Peter was saying this, all of us were weeping with our mother. Seeing us weep, he said, “Now let each of you bear what has been said courageously through fear toward God. Your father did not die today, but long ago, as you yourselves said in conjecture.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν ἔλεγεν τεθνάναι γέροντα, αὐτὸς ἦν (ἐξ ὧν ἔλεγεν) ὁ ὑμέτερος πατήρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the old man he said had died was your father
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter here identifies the reportedly deceased subject of the story, not yet explicitly the living speaker himself. The old man’s later identity is not read backward into Peter’s present assertion.
The concrete salt-sharing expression is retained in this meal context rather than made an unspecified conversation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἐβουλήθην τὸ καθ’ ὑμᾶς αὐτῷ συναντιβαλεῖν, μέχρις ἂν ὑμῖν προσανάθωμαι.
lexical_decisions.chosen: I did not wish to bring up your circumstances with him until I had consulted you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The personal dative αὐτῷ identifies the old man as the participant in the contemplated conversation. συναντιβαλεῖν suggests bringing accounts together for comparison or exchanging information; “compare your circumstances in discussion with him” is a more explicit alternative. Peter withholds that exchange with the man, not merely an internal comparison with an account.

passages.text: When Peter said this, my mother could not bear it and cried aloud, “Alas, husband! Loving us, you yourself died without judgment, while we live, see the light, and partake of food.” As this single lament ended, the old man came in. Just as he was about to ask the cause of the cry, he looked at the woman and said, “Alas! What does this mean? Whom do I see?” He approached, looked more closely, was seen in turn, and embraced her. Both were fainting from sudden joy; though they wanted to speak to one another, they were seized with speechlessness from their insatiable joy and could not keep control. But after a little while my mother said, “I have you, Faustus, sweetest to me in every way! How are you alive, when just a little earlier we heard you were dead? But these are our sons: Faustinus, Faustinianus, and Clement.” When she said this, we three fell upon him and covered him with kisses, faintly recalling his appearance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡμᾶς ἀγαπῶν ἀκριτὶ αὐτὸς μὲν ἐτελεύτησας
lexical_decisions.chosen: Loving us, you yourself died without judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches ἀκριτί to ἐτελεύτησας, dying, reading the lament as contrasting his death with their continuing life. The adverb may mean without discrimination, decision, or deliberation; “without judgment” does not assert that a tribunal, hearing, or legal proceeding was involved. A material alternative attaches it to ἡμᾶς ἀγαπῶν: “loving us without discrimination/deliberation, you yourself died.” That reading characterizes the manner of his love rather than his dying. The immediate focus on death in the lament motivates the main attachment, but the proximity to the preceding participle leaves the alternative viable and not uniquely settled.
The verb can denote dying or perishing. Their subsequent speech and embrace support deathlike faintness or loss of consciousness here, not actual death followed by resurrection.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀμαυρῶς πως τὴν μορφὴν αὐτοῦ ἀνεφέρομεν
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean bringing back or reproducing. Their childhood separation supports recollection of his appearance rather than verbally describing it for an unstated audience.

source_issues.issue: The supplied edition prints a period after the elided μετ’. The English construes μετ’ with οὐ πολὺ as “after a little while” despite that intervening punctuation. This is a disclosed printed/editorial feature; the Greek period is not deleted or claimed as an OCR error, and no lacuna or missing word is restored.
